limits: An ADC maps a continuous or analog signal range to discrete digital codes. With a fixed number of levels, quantization error depends on where the levels are placed and on the distribution of values. A uniform quantizer allocates equal intervals; a learned quantizer places levels according to observed values.

ReLU maps negative values to zero and clamping limits values to a range. These operations can accumulate samples near zero or a clamp boundary. If those boundary samples dominate clustering, the learned centers may describe the boundary mass while giving too few useful levels to the interior or to less frequent but important values.

BS-KMQ removes boundary outliers before K-means clustering and derives nonlinear references for the ADC. That can make the level placement more informative for the retained distribution, but the removal rule, threshold, calibration distribution and treatment of values returned at inference must be specified. An outlier removed during calibration can still occur during deployment and saturate or map to a poor code.

A reconfigurable in-memory nonlinear ADC changes its reference levels or transfer function while staying coupled to the CIM array. The implementation must account for reference storage, switching, calibration, conversion time, comparator behavior, input range, noise, mismatch and the energy of the reconfiguration. Fewer ADC levels can reduce conversion cost, but only if the quantization error and analog nonidealities remain within the model's tolerance.

limits: A CIM macro performs part of a neural operation inside or next to the memory array. The macro has finite rows, columns, precision and conversion capacity, so a model larger than the available storage must be tiled and its weights, activations and partial sums moved between macros or external memory.

A dataflow defines where weights, activations and partial sums reside and when each moves. At the macro level it can choose which operand is stationary and how bit planes are processed. At the macro-array level it can choose tiling, placement, interconnect routes, reduction order and reuse across macros. These choices change array utilization, buffer occupancy, transfer volume, conversion count and synchronization.

Systematic exploration is useful only when the search space contains the relevant hardware and mapping choices. A cycle-accurate simulator can estimate stalls and movement for a defined architecture, while post-layout PPA analysis can estimate physical area, timing and power for a defined implementation. Neither result is independent of the macro model, peripheral assumptions, calibration and technology library.

Large LLMs make off-chip movement important because weights and activations may not fit in the CIM array. An efficient mapping must include weight loading, activation movement, partial-sum accumulation, sequence or batch reuse and output transfer. A dataflow that is best for a model fitting on chip may be poor when the model is partitioned across memory levels.

The description establishes a framework and evaluation method but reports no numerical TOPS/W, area, accuracy, search cost, peripheral overhead or dataflow ranking. Results may depend on model, precision, array capacity, technology and calibrated macro behavior; the record is evidence of a systematic exploration proposal, not a universal CIM dataflow conclusion.

limits: Block floating point stores a shared scale for a group of values and lower-precision mantissas or integers for the members. MANTIS uses MXINT values for the analog MAC and applies FP8 scaling digitally. This separates high-throughput integer accumulation from dynamic-range adjustment, but the scale path must remain synchronized with the vector, handle zero and overflow, and account for scale storage and movement. A result for the integer MAC alone does not establish the cost of the complete scaled operation.

Charge-domain accumulation combines analog charge contributions before the ADC resolves the result. The ADC's effective number of bits, capacitor mismatch, thermal noise, nonlinearity, reference accuracy and input range determine whether the accumulated value is distinguishable. The 8-bit nominal ADC and 7.62 ENOB must be interpreted with the accumulation depth, calibration, voltage and operating conditions.

Reusing the SAR ADC DAC as both a bit-plane accumulator and part of conversion can reduce duplicated circuitry, but it couples accumulation timing, capacitor settling, DAC linearity and ADC conversion scheduling. SRAM compatibility also requires the macro to fit the foundry memory constraints while adding compute cells and mixed-signal peripherals; compatibility alone does not establish equal density, yield or reliability to a standard SRAM.

limits: A DRAM bitline pair carries complementary signals associated with a cell and its reference or sensing path. A normal access uses the pair to develop a small voltage difference that a sense amplifier resolves and restores. In-memory computation changes the activation and combination sequence so the electrical state represents a logic result, making charge sharing, leakage, coupling and timing part of logical correctness.

Dual-rail signaling uses both complementary rails instead of leaving one rail underused. Full-swing signals can create a larger sensing margin than a small analog difference under some conditions, but the two rails require matched devices, additional contacts and control. Mismatch or unequal loading can reduce the expected benefit.

DRCA-OR and DRCA-XOR are named dual-contact compute cells. The evaluation must show the input encoding, activation sequence, sense-amplifier decision, restore behavior and how the cell's physical changes affect retention and ordinary DRAM access. A logic truth table is not enough to establish operation across process, voltage, temperature and disturbance conditions.

Concurrent operations on one bitline pair can reduce the number of sequential activations needed for a compound bitwise function. Concurrency is valid only if intermediate states remain distinguishable and the sense/restore sequence does not corrupt inputs needed by later operations. The timing schedule, reset or restore policy and data dependencies determine whether the throughput benefit survives in a full array.

The source reports a 2.29× failure-rate reduction and better average basic-bitwise performance against a prior PIM design, but does not expose absolute failure rates, voltage margins, fault distribution, temperature, process variation, latency, energy, area or peripheral costs. Dual rails and extra contacts may increase array area and activation energy; the record establishes a reported DRAM-PIM scheme, not silicon-level reliability or complete system efficiency.

limits: A sequence pair uses two orderings to encode relative positions of blocks. The ordering is discrete: changing one item can change several geometric relationships, so a small numerical gradient is not directly defined on the original representation.

Gumbel–Sinkhorn relaxation replaces a hard permutation or ordering with a smooth approximation that can be differentiated. During optimization the relaxed object may not correspond to a legal discrete placement. The temperature, rounding rule and gap between relaxed and discrete objectives determine whether the optimized result survives conversion.

Area, wirelength and symmetry can be placed in one differentiable objective, but their weights determine the search outcome. A short wirelength can conflict with matching, routing resources or parasitic limits. The optimization must expose objective weights and evaluate the final legalized layout under the actual analog constraints.

MILP legalization enforces exact geometric and symmetry constraints after the relaxed optimization. It can move blocks away from the relaxed solution, make the problem infeasible or consume substantial runtime. The post-legalization objective and any repair cost must be included; legalization is not evidence that the relaxed candidate was already valid.

The description names industrial OTA benchmarks and claims better placement quality, post-layout performance and runtime than state-of-the-art placers, but reports no numeric result, constraint-satisfaction rate, legalization failures, solver budget, extraction setup, parasitic metric or circuit-quality condition. limits: A DRC rule defines a geometric condition such as minimum width, spacing or enclosure. A logarithmic-domain design represents magnitude through a logarithm so multiplication-like operations can become additions or shifts. Shift-add decomposition reduces a complex operation only if the approximation meets the model's numerical requirements.

Unifying functions requires identifying a shared internal representation and the function-specific coefficients, branches or sequences that produce each output. Dynamic dataflow reconfiguration can reduce duplicated units while adding control, routing, configuration storage and transition cost.

Activation quality must be evaluated at the network output, not only by local numerical error. baselines: Exact bound under any work-conserving schedule
Prior analysis using deterministic warp paths

Single-context ablations versus the full combination of design document, AST and RTL summary.

fields.problem: At RF/mm-wave frequencies, layout parasitics, coupling, substrate loss, routing geometry and power delivery alter circuit behavior, so schematic-only optimization can miss post-layout gain, noise, frequency and power targets while requiring expensive manual iteration.
fields.method_or_artifact: Four-stage COmPOSER flow: physics-based active sizing plus random-forest/k-NN EM-aware passive optimization; DRC-clean primitive generation; MILP placement, A* routing, pad and PDN synthesis; Cadence EMX/Spectre post-layout validation with targeted constraint tightening and re-synthesis.
fields.workload_or_benchmark: 65 nm CMOS RF/mm-wave LNAs and Class-A PAs up to 60 GHz; four LNA designs and three PA designs; 80,000 spiral inductor EM samples generated and simulated in Cadence EMX; Nangate or other non-target technologies are not used for the reported circuit tables.
fields.hardware_or_process_assumptions: Commercial 65 nm process kit, Cadence EMX, Calibre extraction and Spectre; 1.1 V LNA and 1.2 V PA table conditions; Gurobi MILP at 10^-3 gap; typical 28–30-module layouts with about 2.3k variables and 3.3k constraints. Passive model, PDK, routing and EM results were not reproduced here.
baselines: Manual RF design, including a reported approximately 70-hour 40 GHz LNA design
Layout-oblivious schematic-only sizing in the EM ablation
Selected prior/manual LNA table entries where the process, topology and objective are sufficiently visible
metrics: Passive model: 80k inductors generated and EM-simulated over 24 hours; 200-tree random forest reports R² > 0.999 for inductance/quality/resonance outputs; EM optimizer reports within 0.4% of EM simulation and >1000× speedup for that step.

PA post-layout table: PA1/2/3 gain 14.7/16/13.6 dB, Psat 9.5/6.7/6.8 dBm, bandwidth 10.2/5.1/8.3 GHz, DC power 51.3/53.0/63.5 mW, maximum PAE 25/7.5/6.4%, area 0.220/0.254/0.282 mm², runtime 2.31/3.25/3.74 min; all stable.

Runtime: LNA total 23.58 min and PA total 40.10 min including EM/SPICE verification versus about 70 hours manual LNA; one-time passive data generation about 24 hours. Layout-oblivious 60 GHz ablation shifts PA/LNA center frequency to 45/40 GHz, loses 4.6/3.4 dB gain, loses 4 dB PA output power and worsens LNA NF by 1.75 dB.
limits: Post-layout results are simulation and extraction results in one commercial 65 nm process kit, not fabricated-silicon measurements or universal transfer across PDKs, frequencies, topologies and passive structures.

The manual comparison is not fully matched for every table column; one cited LNA uses bandwidth extension and trades gain/NF. Productivity includes a separately listed one-time 24-hour EM-data generation cost and differs in human intervention, stopping rules and verification boundaries.

Surrogate accuracy and runtime do not establish complete circuit correctness; constraint retries, failed candidates, post-layout convergence, repository execution and independent reproduction remain open. The 100–300× claim is a reported workflow turnaround comparison, not a universal per-simulation speedup.

fields.problem: Technology mapping heuristics are hand-designed software, and improving their area/delay tradeoff through LLM-guided code evolution requires preserving output equivalence while controlling search and evaluation cost.
fields.method_or_artifact: MappingEvolve uses Planner, Evolver and Evaluator roles to propose structured changes to technology-mapping code, compile the candidate mapper, map circuits, check logical equivalence, and score normalized area and delay. The released artifact includes a proactive evolution driver and author-provided run histories.
fields.workload_or_benchmark: Eleven ISCAS85 circuits form the evolution suite; EPFL circuits after ABC `compress2` and ASAP7 evaluation form the reported evaluation suite. The assessed loop uses 30 outer iterations × 3 inner iterations, compared with 90 direct-evolution iterations.
fields.hardware_or_process_assumptions: Selected artifact conditions: Ubuntu 22.04, Xeon Gold 6226R and 256 GB memory; ABC `&nf` and mockturtle `map` are named baselines. Compilation and ABC CEC equivalence precede QoR evaluation; post-route behavior and process/library transfer are not established.
baselines: Strong technology-mapping baselines named by the official description
metrics: Table 2 average ratios to ABC: DeepSeek-V3 area 0.8996, delay 1.0571, mapper runtime 1.755; GPT-5 area 0.8996, delay 1.0369, mapper runtime 1.6557.
The assessed objective is 0.5 × normalized area reduction + 0.5 × normalized delay reduction; area reduction therefore can coexist with slower mapped-circuit delay or longer mapper runtime.

The official description reports 10.04% area reduction versus ABC, 7.93% versus mockturtle, and 46.6%–96.0% S_overall improvement; these headline values remain conditioned on source-to-result reconciliation.
limits: Table averages show a tradeoff, not dominance: the visually crosschecked ratios reduce area while increasing average delay and mapper runtime. Composite QoR is not execution speedup.

Equal iteration counts do not establish equal wall-clock time, token/API cost, stochastic search opportunity or total engineering cost. Repeated seeds, dispersion, model versions, held-out protocol and timeout/equivalence-failure handling remain unresolved.

The pinned driver updates `best_state` on reward improvement before acceptance and can restore that state after rejection; this is a source-level control-flow concern, not evidence that a published circuit was invalid. The inspected author logs show no outer-loop reversion in three selected runs, but they are not independently authenticated.

No mapping experiment or repository code was executed here. Equivalence of evaluated netlists does not prove arbitrary future outputs, post-route quality, process transfer or universal mapper improvement.

rows.reason: Reconciles the captured abstract card with the full arXiv preprint; separates HLS logic debugging from syntax repair, generated mutation supervision from natural bugs, identification granularities from exact-snippet correction, and benchmark results from hardware-level validity.

fields.problem: HLS code can compile while implementing the wrong function. Debugging without reliable test cases requires locating the faulty code, identifying its logic-bug type and producing a correction; circuit data for training is scarce.
fields.method_or_artifact: HLSDebugger releases an approximately 300K-sample labeled dataset and fine-tunes a CodeT5-Large encoder–decoder. The encoder predicts bug type and token locations; its representations guide a cross-attending decoder that generates the corrected snippet. A weighted joint loss trains bug type, imbalanced token location and correction generation together.
fields.workload_or_benchmark: A random 2,000-sample evaluation subset from an eight-bug-type HLS benchmark: out-of-bounds array access, uninitialized read, out-of-bounds shift, infinite loop, unintended sign extension, incorrect manual loop unrolling, wrong zero initialization and wrong split-buffer half. Training data starts with roughly 30K crawled HLS samples and roughly 10K GPT-3.5 RTL-to-HLS augmentations; about 2K high-Rouge-L-overlap samples are removed from training.
fields.hardware_or_process_assumptions: CodeT5-Large with 24 encoder and 24 decoder transformer layers, 1024-dimensional embeddings and 16-dimensional heads; three-layer MLP prediction heads. Evaluation uses token, line and code-level identification plus strict processed substring matching for correction, with generated length limited to three times the label length. HLS compilation, synthesis, timing, area, power and independent functional/equivalence checking are not part of the reported correction metric.
metrics: Identification: HLSDebugger token precision/recall/F1/ROC area 54.3%/83.5%/0.614/0.935; line precision/recall/F1/ROC area 57.7%/78.4%/0.627/0.923; code-wise top-1/top-5 79.5%/87.6%.
Identification baselines include GPT-4 token precision/recall 12.2%/37.1%, line precision/recall 13.3%/17.5% and code-wise top-1/top-5 19.7%/54.7%.

Correction without the true location: HLSDebugger 37.6%, GPT-4 10.5%, Gemma-7B SFT 15.1%, and HLSEncoder plus Gemma-7B SFT 23.7%. Correction with the ground-truth location supplied: HLSDebugger 49.1%.
limits: The approximately 300K labels are generated through code collection, GPT-3.5 augmentation and prompted bug insertion; the mutation distribution and eight categories do not establish coverage of naturally occurring HLS failures.

Strict substring match measures agreement with the labeled correction after preprocessing, not compilation, functional equivalence, synthesis validity, hardware quality or semantic correctness in an arbitrary surrounding design.

The 2,000-sample random evaluation subset and Rouge-L filtering constrain the reported generalization claim; exact project splits, per-category denominators and semantic contamination outside the threshold remain relevant.

The reported model is not ready for practical debugging according to the paper's own discussion: the best no-location correction rate is 37.6%. Training/inference cost, human effort, held-out projects, naturally occurring bugs and independent HLS-tool validation remain open.

fields.problem: Sub-8-bit quantization can reduce model storage without reducing work on commodity mobile SIMD if the kernel expands values to byte lanes or cannot handle fine-grained scales; quantization can also distort self-attention and task quality.
fields.method_or_artifact: Squat combines entropy-guided and distribution-aligned QAT, token-importance-based 4/8-bit activation quantization, FP16-teacher distillation and a SIMD multi-kernel mixed-precision (MKMP) multiplier with token-control and concatenation support.
fields.workload_or_benchmark: LLaMA-58M and GPT2-97M; zero-shot BLiMP and fine-tuned (Super)GLUE; W8A8, W4A8 and W4A4 plus mixed 4:8 activation ratios. Deployment uses sequence length 128, 1,000 latency iterations, OnePlus 11/Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 and Raspberry Pi 5/BCM2712 quad-core Arm Cortex-A76, all available cores.
fields.hardware_or_process_assumptions: Mobile/edge SIMD with byte-oriented INT8 paths; MKMP concatenates sub-byte operands and recovers intermediate products. Reported latency is ms/token and includes the paper's runtime/compiler path; warmup, thermal controls and exact prefill/decode boundary remain unresolved. No on-device training measurement is established.
metrics: LLaMA-58M BLiMP averages: FP16 74.0, Squat W4A8 74.0 and Squat W4A4 67.8; GPT2-97M W4A4 BLiMP Main averages: FP16 69.9, NIPQ 49.4, PACT 59.7, LLM-QAT 69.1 and Squat 69.2.

LLaMA-58M W4A4 (Super)GLUE average: FP16 71.0, Squat 68.6. Latency at sequence length 128: LLaMA-58M FP16/W4A4 4.54/2.02 ms per token on OnePlus 11 and 15.63/6.78 on Raspberry Pi; GPT2-97M 6.22/2.75 and 23.04/9.74 respectively.

Mixed GPT2-97M mobile 4:8 activation ratios 1:3 and 1:1 report 3.06 and 3.02 ms/token; the table labels their speedups 2.06 and 2.03, while displayed-value division gives 2.03 and 2.06. The saved assessment classifies both as rounding-incompatible under its stated rounding assumption; no values are silently swapped.
limits: Speedup is not an iso-accuracy claim. The tables contain per-task regressions, and the W4A4 averages do not preserve FP16 quality uniformly across BLiMP or (Super)GLUE.

Token ranking, heapsort, concatenation, memory traffic, shifts, result recovery and thread scheduling are part of executable cost; a theoretical half-work or smaller multiplier does not establish half end-to-end latency.

The two GPT2-mobile speedup inconsistencies require raw runs and the author's rounding policy; arithmetic consistency checks are not latency reproduction. Warmup, thermal controls, prefill/decode boundary, version-matched harness and checkpoint/token-selector provenance remain open.

The result is limited to two small models, selected tasks, two edge platforms and the stated configurations. Public code was not executed here; no on-device training, silicon measurement, independent reproduction or universal deployment claim is established.

metrics: Thermal reduction versus Homo-3D at batch 32 and 512/512 input/output: average peak-temperature reduction 3.96 °C, 6.10 °C and 5.99 °C for 48, 60 and 72 cores; frequency-comparison ranges 3.63–5.55 °C, 5.73–9.37 °C and 5.12–7.91 °C.

The 2.85×/2.12×/1.33× comparisons combine heterogeneous cores, 3D bandwidth, thermal response, cache placement and bandwidth sharing; they do not isolate one mechanism or establish transfer to other models, traffic, stacks, cooling systems or baselines.
